summary: This standards-track RFC describes how to configure proactive MPLS-TP Operations, Administration, and Maintenance functions for a label switched path. It does this using a set of TLVs carried by the LSP Ping protocol.

eli5.summary: Before a road starts its automatic health checks, someone has to say how they should work. This uses ping messages to carry those settings.

questions: configure mpls-tp oam with lsp ping
how to configure mpls-tp oam with lsp ping
what is the mpls oam functions tlv
what bfd settings does lsp ping configure
subtitle: How LSP Ping carries the settings that switch on and tune proactive OAM on an MPLS-TP label switched path.

tldr.problem: MPLS Transport Profile paths need proactive monitoring (continuity checks, loss and delay measurement, fault signals), and these functions have to be configured at both ends of each path.
tldr.mechanism: A new MPLS OAM Functions TLV, with flags and nested sub-TLVs, rides in LSP Ping Echo Request and Reply messages to enable and parameterize BFD, performance monitoring and fault management signals.
tldr.outcome: It gives a way to configure proactive OAM without a control plane, defines new error return codes and registers the TLV types, flags and codes with IANA.

facts.label: Function flags
facts.value: C, V, F, L, D, T (bits 0 to 5)

facts.label: Default PM intervals
facts.value: Loss 100 ms, Delay 1000 ms, Test 10 ms

sections.title: Configuring Proactive OAM
sections.content:
The MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) adds Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) functions to MPLS. RFC 5860 sets their requirements. This RFC describes how to configure the proactive ones for a Label Switched Path (LSP) using TLVs carried in LSP Ping (RFC 4379).

Because MPLS-TP must be able to run without a control plane, the options are a Network Management System (NMS), LSP Ping as here, or extensions to RSVP-TE and Targeted LDP. On-demand OAM is out of scope.

The proactive tools are Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD, RFC 6428) for continuity and connectivity checks, Delay Measurement and Loss Measurement (RFC 6374, RFC 6375), and Fault Management Signals (RFC 6427).
sections.eli5: Some roads in a network get automatic checkups. This document is the form you fill out to say which checkups to run and how often.

sections.title: How Configuration Works
sections.content:
LSP Ping, or alternatively RSVP-TE, enables OAM functions by setting flags in the MPLS OAM Functions TLV. Sub-TLVs can add detailed parameters. Intermediate nodes normally forward these TLVs to the end node untouched. The exception is the Fault Management Signal sub-TLV, which MUST be examined even by intermediate nodes that support the extension.

If a flag is set and its sub-TLVs are absent, the function MUST start with its default settings, which this document leaves out of scope. A sub-TLV present without its flag SHOULD be ignored. If all flags are zero, the TLV is treated as not present. If more than one TLV is in an Echo Request, the first SHOULD be processed and the rest ignored.
sections.eli5: The checklist is passed along the road. Only the end points read most of it. If you tick a box without details, they use the usual settings.

sections.title: The MPLS OAM Functions TLV
sections.content:
The TLV is type 27 and rides in MPLS Echo Request and Reply messages. It has a Length, a 32-bit field of MPLS OAM Function Flags, then sub-TLVs. Undefined flags MUST be zero and unknown flags MUST be ignored.

The registered flags are bit 0 C (Continuity Check), 1 V (Connectivity Verification), 2 F (Fault Management Signal), 3 L (PM/Loss), 4 D (PM/Delay) and 5 T (Throughput). Bits 6 to 30 are unassigned and bit 31 is reserved.

The sub-TLVs are numbered 100 to 104 for BFD and traffic class, 200 to 202 for performance monitoring, 300 for fault management signals and 400 for the Source MEP-ID. Registration in the sub-TLV registry is by Standards Action in the ranges 0-16383 and 32768-49161.
sections.eli5: The checklist starts with a row of switches, one for each kind of checkup. Extra pages hold the details for the ones you switch on.

sections.title: Setting Up BFD Sessions
sections.content:
The BFD Configuration sub-TLV (100) is required if the C flag, the V flag or both are set. BFD MUST run in asynchronous mode with both sides active, or in unidirectional mode. LSP Ping can only bootstrap a session, with timers negotiated later in BFD control messages (flag N), or it can carry the timers directly in a BFD Negotiation Timer Parameters sub-TLV (102), which holds Acceptable Min. Asynchronous TX and RX intervals and the Required Echo TX Interval, all in microseconds.

Other flags choose symmetric timing (S), integrity (I), G-ACh or IP/UDP encapsulation (G, U, with G winning if both are set) and bidirectional mode (B). A BFD Local Discriminator sub-TLV (101) must be included when B is set.

BFD control packets sent in the Associated Channel Header have no end-to-end checksum, so a flipped bit could make an end wrongly conclude the link is down. The Integrity flag turns on BFD Authentication using Keyed SHA1 with an empty key of all zeros, so each packet carries a SHA1 hash that detects errors. For a real pre-shared key, a BFD Authentication sub-TLV (103) names the Auth Type and Auth Key ID. Simple Password SHOULD NOT be used if other types are available, and key exchange is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The heartbeat checker needs to know how often to knock, whether to knock both ways, and whether to use a secret knock. The ping carries those answers.

sections.title: Loss and Delay Measurement
sections.content:
If the L, D or T flag is set, the Performance Monitoring sub-TLV (200) MUST be present, or an "OAM Problem/PM Configuration Error" results. Its flags choose direct or inferred delay and loss, and switch on delay variation (jitter), dyadic, loopback and combined modes, each tied to an error if the egress LSR lacks support.

The PM Loss sub-TLV (201) and PM Delay sub-TLV (202) each carry a timestamp format, a traffic-class flag, an octet-count flag, a Measurement Interval, a Test Interval and a threshold. Defaults are 100 ms (loss) and 1000 ms (delay) for the Measurement Interval, and 10 ms for the Test Interval, as in RFC 6375. The loss threshold counts lost packets per measurement. The delay threshold is a two-way delay in milliseconds. Throughput uses the loss tool, so the same sub-TLV applies.
sections.eli5: You can ask the road to count lost cars and time how long trips take, and say how often to check and when to raise an alarm.

sections.title: Fault Signals and Source MEP-ID
sections.content:
To configure Fault Management Signals, the F flag MUST be set and the FMS sub-TLV (300) included to change defaults. Its flags are E (enable AIS and Lock Report signaling, default enabled), S (ask a Server MEP to send them on the client LSP, default 0) and T (set a specific timer, default 0). The Refresh Timer MUST be between 1 and 20 seconds. When working and protection paths are both configured they SHOULD use identical E, T and timer settings.

The Traffic Class sub-TLV (104) sets the TC in the top label stack entry for periodic continuity messages or fault messages. If absent, the choice is local. The Source MEP-ID sub-TLV (400) holds a 32-bit Source Node ID, a 16-bit Tunnel ID and a 16-bit LSP ID.
sections.eli5: If a road breaks, nearby stations send alarm messages. This part says whether to send them, how often to repeat, and who identifies the sender.

sections.title: Errors for Unsupported Settings
sections.content:
When the egress LSR cannot honor a requested setting, it MUST return an "OAM Problem" return code in the Echo Reply. IANA assigned sub-codes 21 to 34, covering BFD version, encapsulation, authentication type and key ID, timestamp format, delay and loss modes, delay variation, dyadic, loopback and combined modes, fault management signaling, failure to create a fault management association, and PM configuration errors.

An ingress may combine several TLVs in one Echo Request. If the egress supports none of the requested modes it MUST report the first unsupported one in the list. If any requested configuration is unsupported, the egress SHOULD NOT process the OAM configuration TLVs in that request.
sections.eli5: If the far end cannot do something you asked, it writes back exactly which thing it could not do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Signaling OAM parameters adds risks beyond those in RFC 4379. An attacker could request high-frequency liveliness monitoring of many LSPs aimed at one network element and overload it. Implementations should know their OAM resources and MAY refuse new configurations that would overload a node. Resource policies may share OAM capacity fairly across LSPs.

Security for LSP Ping must already be in place. Exchanging keys for OAM is out of scope and assumed to use an off-line mechanism or an established secure key exchange protocol. Security of the configured protocols is discussed in RFC 5880, RFC 5884, RFC 6374, RFC 6427 and RFC 6428.
sections.eli5: If a bully asks for too many checkups, a station could get tired out, so it may say no. Secret keys are handed out some other safe way.
